findings.title: Redaction word-boundary miss: underscore-prefixed env var names silently pass through
findings.description: The key=value pattern uses \b (word boundary) before the keyword. In Python re, underscore is a word character, so \bsecret does NOT match in AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, DB_PASSWORD, ACCESS_TOKEN, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, API_TOKEN, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, or TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN. These are extremely common env var names that Claude Code will encounter in .env files and shell commands. The value is logged verbatim.
findings.attack_path: Claude runs `printenv` or reads a .env file containing AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=AKIA... or DB_PASSWORD=hunter2. The PostToolUse hook captures tool_response.stdout. _redact_value processes the string. The kv pattern searches for \b(password|...) and finds no match because _ precedes the keyword. The raw secret is written to ~/.claude/logs/tool-calls-YYYY-MM-DD.jsonl.
findings.evidence: python3 -c "import re; kv=re.compile(r'(?i)\\b(password|passwd|secret|token|api[_-]?key)(\\s*[:=]\\s*)([^\\s,;\'\"]{3,})'); print(bool(kv.search('AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=abc123')))" => False; print(bool(kv.search('DB_PASSWORD=mysecret'))) => False; print(bool(kv.search('ACCESS_TOKEN=mysecret'))) => False; print(bool(kv.search('secret=abc123'))) => True
findings.fix: Change \b(password|...) to (?:^|[^\w])(password|...) or use a lookbehind (?<![\w]). Alternatively, add a second pattern that matches the same keywords when they appear as the last segment of an UPPER_SNAKE_CASE name: (?i)(?:^|_)(password|passwd|secret|token|api[_-]?key)(\s*[:=]\s*)([^\s,;'"]{3,}).

findings.title: Missing credential formats: Stripe sk_live_, Slack xoxb-, GCP service-account private_key, AWS secret access key (raw)
findings.description: Four credential formats that could appear in tool output are not caught by any pattern. (1) Stripe secret keys: sk_live_XXX and sk_test_XXX use underscore after sk, not hyphen; the OpenAI pattern requires sk-. (2) Slack bot tokens: xoxb-NNN-NNN-XXX have no matching prefix. (3) GCP service account JSON: the private_key field value is a PEM block starting with -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----; no PEM pattern exists. (4) AWS secret access key (the 40-char base64-like string that pairs with AKIA) has no standalone pattern; it is caught only when the surrounding key name matches, which SEC-001 shows fails for AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=.
findings.attack_path: Claude is asked to configure a Stripe integration and echoes the secret key in a curl command or tool output. The Stripe key sk_live_AbCdEfGh... does not match \bsk-[A-Za-z0-9]{40,80}\b because the separator is underscore. The key is logged in plaintext.
findings.fix: Add patterns: (1) Stripe: re.compile(r'\bsk_(live|test)_[A-Za-z0-9]{24,}\b') -> ***STRIPE_KEY***. (2) Slack: re.compile(r'\bxox[bparos]-[0-9A-Za-z-]{10,}\b') -> ***SLACK_TOKEN***. (3) PEM block: re.compile(r'-----BEGIN [A-Z ]+-----[\s\S]+?-----END [A-Z ]+-----') -> ***PEM_BLOCK***. Note: the kv pattern with the SEC-001 fix would catch GCP private_key= context if the env var appears as private_key=...; standalone PEM blocks still need an explicit pattern.

findings.title: safety-block.sh quote-stripping does not protect against $() or backtick subshell expansion wrapping a blocked path
findings.description: The script strips single- and double-quoted strings before pattern matching to reduce false positives. However, $() and backtick subshell expressions are not stripped. A command like `rm -rf $(echo /)` strips to `rm -rf $(echo )` after removing '/', and the regex that checks for `rm ... /$` or `rm ... / ` no longer matches because the literal / is gone. The block is bypassed. This is noted in the script as an approximation, and the attack requires Claude to be deceived into running such a command. The deny block in settings.json (`Bash(rm -rf *)`) provides a separate backstop for the exact rm -rf pattern; however that Bash deny rule is glob-matched on the raw command and may also not cover subshell-expansion variants depending on Claude Code's matching semantics.
findings.attack_path: Attacker controls a git repository README that contains a shell snippet. Claude is asked to follow setup instructions and runs `rm -rf $(echo /)`. safety-block.sh strips the empty string (no quoted tokens in this version) -- wait, `echo /` has no quotes, so no stripping occurs and the `/` is literal. Variant: `rm -rf $(echo '/' | cat)` -> after strip: `rm -rf $(echo  | cat)` -- the literal / is removed.
findings.evidence: Python simulation: cmd = "rm -rf $(echo '/')"; stripped = re.sub("'[^']*'", '', cmd) => 'rm -rf $(echo )'; re.search(r'rm\s+(-\w*r\w*f)\w*\s+(/$|/\s)', stripped) => None. Block bypassed.
findings.fix: This is a known class of limitation for regex-based shell parsing. The primary mitigation is the settings.json deny block `Bash(rm -rf *)`. For defense-in-depth, add a separate safety-block.sh rule that matches $() or backtick wrapping of paths after the rm -rf flags, or add a rule that blocks any rm -rf where the path segment contains $( or `. Document that the $(echo ...) variant is a known gap.

findings.title: Stop hook sends full Claude response (potentially containing user data) to a second model -- undocumented privacy implication
findings.description: The anti-rationalization Stop hook uses type: prompt. Per Claude Code documentation, this sends the hook prompt concatenated with Claude's final response to a fast model (Haiku). Claude's response may contain content from the user's codebase, file contents, API responses, or other sensitive project data that was processed during the session. This is a data-handling implication that differs from command-type hooks. Neither HOOKS.md nor README.md documents that the response text is transmitted to a second model API call, nor that users should be aware of what their response may contain.
findings.attack_path: Not a traditional attack path -- this is a data-handling disclosure gap. A user working on a confidential project may not realize that Claude's response summarizing proprietary code or internal architecture is sent to Haiku as part of the Stop hook. The hook runs on every session stop, not just when rationalization is detected.
findings.evidence: settings.json line 127: type: prompt. HOOKS.md line 87: 'Sends Claude final response to a fast model'. README.md Anti-rationalization section: no mention of the response content being transmitted. Neither file notes that this constitutes an additional API call containing response content.
findings.fix: Add a note to both HOOKS.md and README.md's Anti-rationalization section: 'Note: this hook transmits Claude's full response text to an additional model API call on every session stop. If your session involved sensitive or proprietary content, that content may appear in the response and will be included in this API call.'

findings.title: Temp pair files written with open() (mode 0o666 pre-umask) rather than O_CREAT with explicit 0o600
findings.description: The pre-event handler writes a timing pair file to /tmp/claude-tool-<session_hash> using Python's open(pair_path, 'w'), which creates the file with mode 0o666 minus umask (typically 0o644 on macOS). The pair file contains a call_id and a float Unix timestamp. On a multi-user machine, other local users could read these files and infer when Claude tool calls are occurring and correlate them by session. The log file itself (line 102) uses os.open with explicit 0o644, which is consistent with intended read access. The pair file is transient (deleted on post), but there is a race window.
findings.attack_path: On a shared macOS machine where multiple users have access to /tmp, a local attacker polls /tmp/claude-tool-* to detect Claude Code activity timing and session IDs. The hash in the filename is SHA-256 of tool_input which may contain sensitive parameter values -- even though the hash itself is truncated to 16 hex chars, the filename pattern leaks that a specific tool invocation with that exact input occurred.
findings.evidence: log_tool_call.py line 178: open(pair_path, 'w') -- no explicit mode, subject to umask. Log file at line 102: os.open(path, O_WRONLY|O_APPEND|O_CREAT, 0o644). Pair file not created with os.open and explicit 0o600.
findings.fix: Replace open(pair_path, 'w') with: fd = os.open(pair_path, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_TRUNC, 0o600); f = os.fdopen(fd, 'w'). This restricts pair files to owner-only read/write. The log directory itself (0o755) and log files (0o644) have broader read access which is likely intentional for local analytics use.

findings.title: settings.json deny rules: Edit permission missing for credential files that have Write deny; ~/.config/gcloud and ~/.netrc unprotected
findings.description: Two categories of gap. (1) Asymmetric Edit/Write coverage: ~/.aws/**, ~/.gnupg/**, ~/.config/gh/**, ~/.git-credentials, ~/.npmrc, ~/.pypirc, ~/.gem/credentials, ~/.kube/**, ~/.docker/config.json all have Write deny and/or Read deny but NO Edit deny. Claude Code's Edit tool can overwrite file content and may not be blocked by a Write deny rule if the file is modified via Edit. (2) Missing paths: ~/.config/gcloud/** (Google Cloud SDK credentials, application_default_credentials.json) has no Read, Write, or Edit deny. ~/.netrc (used by curl, git, pip for storing credentials in plaintext) has no deny. ~/.config/anthropic/** (Anthropic CLI config, potentially containing API keys) has no deny.
findings.attack_path: For (1): Claude uses the Edit tool to append a malicious SSH key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys or overwrite ~/.aws/credentials. Write deny is set for ~/.aws/** but not Edit deny. If Claude Code distinguishes these tools, the Edit path is open. For (2): Claude is asked to run gcloud commands that fail and is told to check credentials; it reads ~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json which contains OAuth2 tokens.
findings.evidence: settings.json: Edit deny lines are only ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, ~/.ssh/**. Write deny covers ~/.aws/**, ~/.gnupg/**, ~/.git-credentials etc. but Edit deny for these paths is absent. ~/.config/gcloud/** not mentioned anywhere in deny block.
findings.fix: (1) Add Edit deny rules mirroring all Write deny rules: Edit(~/.aws/**), Edit(~/.gnupg/**), Edit(~/.config/gh/**), Edit(~/.git-credentials), Edit(~/.npmrc), Edit(~/.pypirc), Edit(~/.gem/credentials), Edit(~/.docker/config.json), Edit(~/.kube/**). (2) Add Read, Write, Edit deny for: ~/.config/gcloud/**, ~/.netrc, ~/.config/anthropic/**. Consider Read(~/.netrc) in particular as it stores plaintext credentials.

residual_risks.description: The Authorization header pattern uses [^*,;'"\r\n]{3,} for the value class, which allows spaces. This means 'Authorization: Bearer tok1 tok2 tok3' is fully consumed into a single *** replacement. This is correct behavior (the entire header value is redacted) but it also means the pattern is greedy and will consume trailing text on the same line that isn't actually part of the credential. This is benign from a security standpoint (over-redaction) but could affect log usefulness. No exploitable path.

The log file at ~/.claude/logs/tool-calls-YYYY-MM-DD.jsonl is world-readable (0o644, drwxr-xr-x directory). On a single-user macOS machine this is standard. On a shared machine, all local users can read the full tool call history including redacted args and output. This is acceptable given the single-developer use case documented in the spec but would be a concern in a shared environment.

The install.sh jq merge uses jq -s '.[0] as $existing | .[1] as $new | $existing * $new | ...' against a user-controlled backup file. If ~/.claude/settings.json contained a crafted deeply-nested JSON structure designed to exploit jq's object merge semantics (e.g., injecting a malicious hook command), that structure could be merged into the installed settings. However, since the source file is the user's own existing settings, this is self-targeted and not an exploitable path from an external attacker. The threat model for settings.json is user-trusted.

The OpenAI key pattern \bsk-[A-Za-z0-9]{40,80}\b would also match Anthropic keys that don't use the sk-ant- prefix (if Anthropic ever changes their key format). This overlap is benign -- the key would be replaced with ***OPENAI_KEY*** instead of ***ANTHROPIC_KEY***, which still achieves redaction.

testing_gaps.description: No test in test-redaction.sh covers underscore-prefixed env var names (AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, DB_PASSWORD, ACCESS_TOKEN). The test suite only checks standalone keyword=value forms like password=foo, not UPPER_SNAKE_CASE variants.
No test covers the Stripe sk_live_ / sk_test_ key format. The existing tests check sk-ant- (Anthropic) and sk- (OpenAI) but not sk_live_ with underscore separator.
No test covers the Edit-vs-Write deny rule asymmetry. The settings-valid test checks that hook paths exist but does not assert that every Write deny path also has a corresponding Edit deny.

No test verifies that the Stop hook type:prompt fires only when the response contains rationalization patterns vs. on every session end. The current configuration sends the response on every Stop event regardless of content, which is a correctness issue separate from security but affects the frequency of data transmission documented in SEC-004.
